prompt.context: Funguy Corporation is a small producer and wholesaler of agricultural fungicides. After a yearly financial review, they find one of their proprietary products, Formula X, is likely to be operating at a loss.
prompt.question: They ask you to quantify the exact loss and find options on how to return Formula X to profitability.

clarifying_info.a: Large international competitors exist for all products.
The market is mature and growing at the rate of inflation, but demand for Formula X specifically is growing at a greater rate.

clarifying_info.q: What is special about Formula X?
clarifying_info.a: It is a new product that is very effective because fungi have not yet developed resistances. It is primarily used on soybeans and other legumes, and is patented with 10 years remaining on the patent.

clarifying_info.q: What type of business is Funguy?
clarifying_info.a: Primarily a producer and wholesaler. They own a production plant and several distribution centers. Business is conducted via several-year-long contracts with both suppliers and buyers.

exhibits.title: Formula X Production Process
exhibits.shows: A diagram of the Formula X production process, showing the sequence of equipment: Hoppers, Mixer, Granulator, Screens, and Scrubber with material flows between each stage.
exhibits.data: Process flow diagram with labeled equipment stages and mass flow arrows; specific quantities to be provided by interviewer

framework: Revenues: Price x Volume — current price per kg of Formula X, current sales volume, potential licensing revenue
Costs: Fixed costs (infrastructure, CapEx, insurance) and Variable costs (labor/MISC per batch, ingredient COGS, scrubber operating cost)
Operations: Production process efficiency, batch structure, capacity utilization, waste/reject rates
Other Considerations: Legal/patent/compliance, competitive dynamics, market growth and agricultural trends, geography, potential cannibalization from other Funguy products

questions.prompt: Quantify the current profitability loss for Formula X (Question 1)
questions.guidance: Candidate should walk through revenue and cost components per batch. Key is understanding the production process to correctly calculate ingredient costs, yield, scrubber trigger, and total cost. Should solve in per-batch or per-day terms. Answer: losing $5,000 per batch or $10,000 per day.

math.setup: Revenue per batch = final product kg x $200/kg. Costs per batch = ingredients + MISC/labor + allocated scrubber cost. Must correctly calculate mass flows through each process stage.
steps: Inputs per batch: 250 kg Ingredient A @ $100/kg = $25,000; 1,000 kg Ingredient B @ $100/kg = $100,000; total ingredient cost = $125,000
Total mass entering Granulator: 250 + 1,000 = 1,250 kg
Granulator: 20% lost as dust/vapor = 250 kg to scrubber; 1,000 kg exits to Screens
Screens: 5% unusable = 50 kg to scrubber; 15% size-rejected = 150 kg reject pile; 80% = 800 kg final product
Revenue per batch: 800 kg x $200/kg = $160,000
Total scrubber waste per batch: 250 + 50 = 300 kg
At 2 batches/day: 600 kg total scrubber waste per day; 600 > 500 threshold, and must end 24h completely clean, so scrubber runs twice; cost = 2 x $20,000 = $40,000/day = $20,000 per batch allocated
MISC/labor: $20,000 per batch
Total daily loss: -$5,000 x 2 batches = -$10,000

questions.prompt: What is the effect of running three batches per day on operating profit? (Question 3)
questions.guidance: Candidate should identify that the key cost advantage is the scrubber: 3 batches produce 900 kg of waste/day, which is still below 1,000 kg, so the scrubber still only runs twice — no incremental scrubber cost for the 3rd batch. Labor/MISC increases for the 3rd batch. Net effect: breakeven.

math.setup: Calculate marginal revenue and marginal cost for the 3rd batch. Note the scrubber capacity constraint carefully.
steps: 3rd batch waste: 300 kg additional; total daily waste = 900 kg
900 kg < 1,000 kg threshold, so scrubber still runs exactly twice; scrubber cost unchanged at $40,000/day
3rd batch revenue: 800 kg x $200/kg = $160,000
3rd batch costs: $125,000 ingredients + $25,000 labor/MISC (increases from $20K to $25K for 3rd shift) + $0 incremental scrubber = $150,000
3rd batch marginal profit: $160,000 - $150,000 = +$10,000
Prior daily loss was -$10,000; adding +$10,000 from 3rd batch = $0 breakeven
math.answer: Breakeven ($0 daily profit); marginal cost of 3rd batch is $150,000 vs $160,000 revenue because scrubber still only runs twice

questions.prompt: What is the effect of recycling the size-rejected pellets on long-term operating profit? (Question 4)
questions.guidance: Candidate must identify: (1) reject pile can only be re-injected before the Granulator (best answer: at the Mixer) because Formula X turns from slurry to solid in the Granulator; (2) recycled rejects still lose 20% at Granulator and 5% at Screens (not 15% size-reject since these are already correct-size pellets — actually still lose 20% at granulator); (3) each reject recycle adds 36 kg to scrubber; (4) at 3 batches + 2 reject recycles, scrubber waste = 972 kg < 1,000 kg, so still 2 cycles; (5) a 3rd reject recycle pushes waste over 1,000 kg requiring a 3rd scrubber run at net loss. Maximum 2 reject recycles per day.

math.setup: Per reject recycle batch: 150 kg re-injected at Mixer. Apply granulator loss (20%) then screen loss (20% total = 5% unusable + 15% rejected, but rejected pellets from the recycle are already right size — per casebook, 20% lost at granulator and 20% overall at screens applies; casebook uses 150 x 80% x 80% = 96 kg). Additional scrubber waste = 150 x 20% + 120 x 5% = 30 + 6 = 36 kg per recycle.
steps: 150 kg reject re-injected at Mixer
Through Granulator: 150 x 80% = 120 kg exits; 30 kg to scrubber
Through Screens: 120 x 80% = 96 kg final product; 6 kg to scrubber (5% of 120)
Revenue per reject recycle: 96 kg x $200/kg = $19,200 (no additional ingredient cost)
Additional scrubber waste per reject recycle: 30 + 6 = 36 kg
At 3 batches/day: base scrubber waste = 900 kg; adding 2 reject recycles: 900 + 36 + 36 = 972 kg < 1,000 kg; scrubber still 2 cycles only
Adding a 3rd reject recycle: 972 + 36 = 1,008 kg > 1,000 kg; scrubber needs 3rd cycle costing $20,000; incremental revenue $19,200 < $20,000 cost; net -$800 — not worthwhile
Maximum 2 reject recycles per day
Incremental daily profit from reject recycling: $19,200 x 2 = $38,400/day
math.answer: $19,200 per reject recycle; maximum 2 recycles per day; total incremental $38,400/day; Formula X moves to +$38,400/day at 3 batches + 2 reject recycles

brainstorming.prompt: Brainstorm ways to increase the profitability of Formula X.

categories.name: Supplier (Cost Side)
ideas: Renegotiate pricing on Ingredients A and B
Buy ingredients in bulk to secure volume discounts
Source ingredients with lower unusable content to improve yield

categories.name: Operations
ideas: Run three batches per day to improve fixed cost absorption and exploit scrubber capacity
Recycle size-rejected pellets back into the process (re-inject before Granulator)
Increase operational efficiency to lower MISC and labor costs
Reduce scrubber operating cost through process improvements
Optimize batch scheduling to minimize scrubber cycles

categories.name: Buyer (Revenue Side)
ideas: Renegotiate pricing upward with buyers given product efficacy and patent exclusivity
Sell to retail channels in addition to wholesale
Adjust target market (e.g., expand beyond soybeans/legumes)
Advertise product benefits to increase demand and justify premium pricing
License the Formula X patent to third parties for royalty revenue

recommendation: Run three batches per day: leverages spare scrubber capacity (waste stays under 1,000 kg/day), brings Formula X to breakeven immediately with no capital investment

Introduce recycling of size-rejected pellets: re-inject 150 kg reject pile at the Mixer each batch; generates $19,200 per recycle run with no incremental scrubber cost for up to 2 recycles/day, netting $38,400/day incremental profit and moving Formula X to positive operating profit
risks: Supplier negotiation power limits ability to cut ingredient costs given multi-year contracts
Buyer negotiation power limits ability to raise prices given multi-year contracts
Running 24 hours (3 shifts) leaves no window for necessary maintenance shutdowns, risking unplanned downtime
Patent expires in 10 years, after which competitors can replicate Formula X
Fungi may develop resistances over time, reducing product efficacy and demand
next_steps: Hire additional personnel to staff the 3rd daily batch
Contact buyers and suppliers to confirm adequate supply of ingredients and sufficient buyer demand to absorb increased volume
Request capital investment quotes for retrofitting the plant with reject-recycling equipment
Model long-term unit economics including depreciation of recycling infrastructure
Monitor competitive response from large international competitors
